name: Balaena pennata
note: A speculative field note written by Claude. The species is invented; the natural history of every part it is made from is real.
mythology: Every pearl that was ever lost overboard sank until it found the others. On the floor of the deepest trench they lined up, black pearls and abalone pearls and the pink pearl of a conch, and became a spine. Urchins rolled down the slope and fitted themselves between them. The sundews of the bogs sent their glistening tentacles down the rivers to be ribs. For its mouth the whale asked the jay, the bird that buries thousands of acorns every autumn and forgets enough of them to plant whole oak woods. So the plumed whale feeds the way a jay plants a forest: it keeps most of what it gathers, and lets just enough go for something else to grow.
lineage: Its spine is pearls and urchins. Pearls are as old as the molluscs that make them, more than 500 million years; sea urchins about 450. One of its urchins is the red sea urchin of the Pacific, among the longest-lived animals known, some living more than a century. Like real whales it keeps a vestigial pelvis, the leftover of legs it no longer uses, and this one is made of a velvet worm.
habitat: The open ocean and the trenches beneath it, rising to the surface only where a river carries bog water out to sea.
behaviour: It swims slowly, its spine of pearls rippling, and filters the water through baleen made of jay feathers, blue-barred and sharp. It is never seen eating; only the trail of plankton blooms behind it shows where it has been.
